title: Growing older, staying strong
excerpt: Stay strong, keep moving and make every year count with simple habits that support healthy ageing and an active lifestyle.
seo_title: Growing Older, Staying Strong | Solevo Physio
meta: Simple strength, aerobic and balance habits that support healthy ageing and an active lifestyle, and when to see a physio. Solevo Physio, Brookvale.
image_alt: Older man doing a push-up on dumbbells during a strength workout
body:
You might enjoy playing golf, walking, cycling, travelling, gardening or heading to the gym. But as you get older, you may notice that recovery takes a little longer, certain movements feel more challenging, or maintaining strength requires a little more effort.

The good news is that getting older doesn't mean giving up the activities you love. Regular strength, aerobic and balance exercises can help maintain muscle strength, fitness, mobility and confidence, supporting you to stay active and independent as you age.

How to stay strong and active

  • Keep moving regularly: Walking, cycling, swimming and golf all count. Find activities you enjoy and keep moving.
  • Strength train twice a week: Target your major muscle groups, including your legs, hips, back, chest and arms.
  • Work on your balance: Include balance exercises to improve stability, coordination and confidence.
  • Train for what you enjoy: Tailor your exercise to the activities you want to keep doing.
  • Keep progressing: Gradually increase the weight, repetitions or difficulty as exercises become easier.

When should you see a physiotherapist?

Consider seeing a physiotherapist if pain is limiting your activity, you're noticing changes in your strength or mobility, you're experiencing recurring aches and pains, or you're unsure how to safely start or progress your exercise.

A physiotherapist can assess your movement, identify areas that may benefit from targeted exercise and help develop a program suited to your abilities and goals.

Want to keep doing the things you love? We can help you build a plan to maintain your strength, mobility and confidence, so you can keep moving well at every stage of life. Book an appointment with our team today.

title: You're never too old to get stronger
excerpt: Build strength, improve your energy, and stay active at every stage of life.
seo_title: You're Never Too Old to Get Stronger | Solevo Physio
meta: Strength training for active adults: why it matters as you age, how to train twice a week and progress safely, and when a physio can help. Solevo Physio.
image_alt: Two older adults lifting kettlebells in a gym
body:
Strength training isn't just for athletes or people who want to build muscle. For active adults, strength helps you climb hills, carry your golf clubs, get up from the ground, play sport and manage everyday activities with confidence.

We naturally lose some muscle mass and strength as we age, but regular resistance training can help slow this decline. It's never too late to build strength and improve your physical capacity. The goal isn't necessarily to lift heavy weights; it's to maintain the strength you need to keep doing the things you enjoy.

How to get more from your strength training

  • Train at least twice a week: Consistency matters more than having a complicated program.
  • Train your whole body: Include exercises for your legs, hips, arms, back and core.
  • Make it challenging: Choose a resistance that challenges your muscles while allowing you to maintain good technique.
  • Progress gradually: Increase the weight, repetitions or difficulty as your strength improves.

When should you seek help?

A physio can help if you're new to strength training, recovering from an injury or joint replacement, experiencing pain during exercise, or unsure how to safely progress your training.

title: Returning to golf after a joint replacement
excerpt: Getting back on the course after joint replacement starts with the right recovery, a steady approach, and confidence in every swing.
seo_title: Returning to Golf After a Joint Replacement | Solevo
meta: Getting back to golf after a knee or hip replacement: build walking distance, leg strength and balance, then return to your swing gradually. Solevo Physio.
image_alt: Golfer finishing a swing on a fairway at sunset
body:
For many active people, getting back to golf is an important part of recovery after a knee or hip replacement. But being able to walk comfortably around the house isn't necessarily the same as being ready to walk 18 holes and repeatedly swing a club.

Golf requires leg strength, balance, walking endurance, hip and trunk control, and the ability to manage uneven ground. A gradual return to the course gives your body time to rebuild these qualities while regaining confidence in your operated leg.

How to prepare for getting back on the course

  • Build your walking distance: Gradually increase your walking distance towards what your usual round requires.
  • Rebuild leg and hip strength: Squats, step-ups and targeted hip exercises can help prepare you for the demands of golf.
  • Work on balance: Practice stability and control to help manage uneven ground and slopes.
  • Return to your swing gradually: Once cleared by your surgeon, start with putting and shorter swings before progressing towards a full round.

When should you seek help?

See your physio if you're struggling to regain strength, experiencing ongoing pain, lacking confidence in your operated leg or aren't sure how to progress back to golf.

title: Hip mobility for golf: improve your golf swing
excerpt: Is hip tightness affecting your golf swing? Discover how improving hip mobility, strength and control can help you move more freely on the course.
seo_title: Hip Mobility for Golf: Improve Your Swing | Solevo Physio
meta: Hip tightness affecting your golf swing? How hip mobility, strength and control help you rotate and move freely on the course, and when to see a physio.
image_alt: Golf ball on a tee with a driver behind it
body:
Your hips play an important role in your golf swing, helping you rotate, generate power and maintain control throughout the movement. If your hips are stiff or lack strength, you may find it harder to achieve the positions your swing requires, potentially placing additional demands elsewhere.

You don't need to be incredibly flexible to play good golf. What matters is having enough mobility, strength and control to comfortably move through the positions your swing requires.

How to improve your hip mobility for golf

  • Move regularly: Don't save all your mobility work for right before your round. Regular movement helps maintain mobility.
  • Work on rotation: Include gentle hip and trunk rotation exercises that reflect the movements of your swing.
  • Strengthen your hips: Strong glutes and hip muscles help control your movement and support power through your swing.
  • Warm up before playing: A few minutes of dynamic movement can help prepare your body before your first tee shot.

When should you seek help?

See a physio if hip stiffness is affecting your swing, you're experiencing pain when rotating, or you're noticing difficulty moving comfortably through your swing.

title: Is knee pain taking the fun out of tennis?
excerpt: Experiencing knee pain when playing tennis? Discover how strength, training load and physiotherapy can help you stay active and enjoy the game.
seo_title: Knee Pain From Tennis? What Helps | Solevo Physio
meta: Knee pain when playing tennis? How leg strength, training load, warm-ups and recovery help your knees cope, and when to see a physio. Solevo Physio.
image_alt: Two tennis players ready at the baseline on a hard court
body:
Tennis involves plenty of running, stopping, changing direction and pushing off, all of which place demands on your knees. If you've recently increased your playing time or intensity, you may notice some soreness as your body adjusts to the extra workload.

The good news is that knee pain doesn't necessarily mean you need to stop playing tennis altogether. Understanding what's contributing to your symptoms and gradually building your strength and capacity can help you manage your knee pain and return to the court with greater confidence.

What can help your knees cope with tennis?

  • Build leg strength: Strong quads, hamstrings, glutes and calves help your knees manage the demands of the court.
  • Increase your workload gradually: Avoid suddenly adding extra matches, longer sessions or more intense competition.
  • Don't forget your warm-up: Prepare your legs with dynamic movements before you start playing.
  • Pay attention to recovery: Give your body enough time to recover when increasing your training load.

When should you seek help?

See a physio if knee pain keeps returning, is getting worse, causes swelling, affects your movement or stops you from playing the way you want to.

title: Save your lower back, save your swing
excerpt: Experiencing lower back pain after golf? Discover how strength, mobility and workload management can help you stay comfortable and enjoy your game.
seo_title: Lower Back Pain After Golf? Save Your Swing | Solevo
meta: Lower back pain after a round of golf? How strength, rotation, warm-ups and workload management help you stay comfortable on the course. Solevo Physio.
image_alt: Golfer following through on a swing under a blue sky
body:
If you find yourself experiencing lower back pain after a round of golf, it may be time to look at your strength, mobility and how much golf you're playing.

Golf places repeated demands on your back, particularly through rotation and bending. If your back isn't tolerating your current playing load, you may notice stiffness after a round, pain during your swing or soreness that lingers into the following day.

Back pain doesn't automatically mean you need to give up golf. Understanding what your back can currently tolerate, addressing contributing factors and gradually building your capacity can help you manage symptoms and get more enjoyment out of your game.

How to look after your back on the course

  • Build your strength: Strong legs, hips and trunk muscles can help your body manage the demands of your golf swing.
  • Work on your rotation: Maintaining adequate mobility and control through your hips and upper back helps you move comfortably through your swing.
  • Warm up before your first tee: Don't make your opening drive your warm-up. Prepare your body with some gentle dynamic movements.
  • Manage your workload: If you've had time away from golf, gradually build back up rather than jumping straight into multiple full rounds.

When should you seek help?

See a physio if your back pain keeps returning, affects your swing, persists well after playing or stops you from enjoying your usual rounds.

title: A minor ankle sprain, a major problem
excerpt: An ankle sprain can be more than a one-off injury. Without appropriate rehabilitation, it can lead to ongoing instability and an increased risk of reinjury.
seo_title: Ankle Sprain Rehab: Why It Matters | Solevo Physio
meta: An ankle sprain can be more than a one-off injury. What to do after a sprain, how strength and balance work prevent reinjury, and when to see a physio.
image_alt: Tennis shoes on a court beside a racquet and ball
body:
Ankle sprains occur when the ligaments supporting the ankle joint are stretched or torn. They're incredibly common in field and court sports, so there's a good chance you've experienced one before.

Many players return to sport as soon as the pain settles, but that doesn't necessarily mean their ankle is ready. Strength, balance and coordination may still be reduced, increasing the risk of rolling your ankle again. Without proper rehabilitation, a seemingly minor injury can develop into an ongoing stability problem.

What should you do after an ankle sprain?

  • PEACE & LOVE: Protect, Elevate, Avoid anti-inflammatories, Compress, Educate, Load, Optimism, promote Vascularisation, Exercise.
  • Strapping or bracing: An ankle brace or appropriate strapping can provide support and help reduce the risk of reinjury when returning to sport.
  • Calf and lower limb strength: Calf raises and progressive single-leg exercises help restore strength and function.
  • Balance and proprioception exercises: Single-leg balance and control exercises help improve ankle stability and coordination.

When should you seek help?

See a physio after an ankle sprain, regardless of severity, to assess the injury, guide recovery and reduce the risk of reinjury.

Sprained your ankle? Physio can help you manage your injury, restore strength and stability, and safely guide your return to sport and everyday activities. Book online.

title: Returning to the gym after joint replacement
excerpt: Had a joint replacement? You can still train.
seo_title: Returning to the Gym After Joint Replacement | Solevo
meta: A joint replacement doesn't mean giving up the gym. How to follow early restrictions, rebuild strength and progress your training safely after surgery.
image_alt: Older man doing a core exercise with a medicine ball in a gym
body:
A joint replacement doesn't necessarily mean saying goodbye to the gym. For many active people, getting back to strength training is an important part of returning to the lifestyle they enjoy.

The key is knowing when and how to progress. Your new joint needs time to recover, while your muscles also need to rebuild strength after surgery. The right exercises and progression will depend on your surgery, recovery and individual goals.

Tips for returning to the gym

  • Follow your surgeon's early restrictions: Your initial rehabilitation should take priority.
  • Start with control: Focus on technique, movement quality and rebuilding basic strength before chasing heavy weights.
  • Progress gradually: Increase resistance and exercise difficulty as your strength and confidence improve.
  • Train for your goals: Whether you want to return to golf, tennis, hiking or general gym training, your program should eventually reflect those activities.

When should you seek help?

See a physio if you're unsure what exercises are appropriate, struggling to regain strength, experiencing ongoing pain or swelling, or aren't confident progressing your gym program.

title: Preparing for knee or hip surgery
excerpt: Preparing for joint replacement? Don't wait until surgery day.
seo_title: Preparing for Knee or Hip Surgery: Prehab | Solevo Physio
meta: Preparing for a knee or hip replacement? How pre-surgery physio (prehab) keeps you strong, mobile and ready for rehab. Solevo Physio, Brookvale.
image_alt: Three adults doing kettlebell squats in a gym
body:
If you're preparing for a knee or hip replacement, it's natural to focus on the surgery itself. But what you do before surgery can also be an important part of your recovery.

Going into surgery as strong and active as possible can give you a better starting point for rehabilitation. Pre-surgery physiotherapy, sometimes called prehabilitation, can help you maintain strength, work on mobility and prepare you for the exercises you'll need afterwards. Working on all of these before your surgery is actually linked to better outcomes post surgery.

How to prepare for your surgery

  • Keep moving: Stay as active as your symptoms allow.
  • Maintain your strength: Focus on the muscles around your hips, knees and the rest of your body.
  • Understand your recovery: Knowing what to expect can make the early stages less daunting.

When should you seek help?

Consider seeing a physio before surgery if pain has reduced your activity, you've lost strength, you're unsure what exercises are safe, or you'd like to be better prepared for rehabilitation.

title: Physiotherapy before vs after joint replacement
seo_title: Physio Before vs After Joint Replacement | Solevo Physio
meta: Physio can start before your knee or hip replacement. What physiotherapy looks like before and after surgery, and when to seek help. Solevo, Brookvale.
image_alt: Woman doing a side lunge exercise in a studio
body:
Many people think physiotherapy begins once they've had their knee or hip replacement. But rehabilitation can actually start before you go into hospital.

Before surgery, physiotherapy can help you maintain strength and mobility, stay active where possible and prepare for the exercises and movements you'll need after surgery. After surgery, the focus shifts towards restoring movement, strength, walking ability and confidence before gradually returning to your normal activities.

Think of it as preparing for a project: the stronger and more prepared you are going in, the more you have to work with during recovery.

What does physio look like before and after?

  • Before: Maintain strength, mobility and general fitness within your symptoms and surgical advice.
  • Before: Learn exercises and strategies you'll use during early rehabilitation.
  • After: Restore movement and strength around the new joint.
  • After: Gradually build towards your individual goals, whether that's walking, golf, the gym, travel or sport.

When should you seek help?

Consider seeing a physio before surgery if you're becoming less active or losing strength. After surgery, seek help if you're unsure how to progress, struggling with movement or strength, or want guidance returning to higher-level activities.

Whether you're preparing for surgery or already recovering, you don't have to navigate the process alone. Emma can help you build a rehabilitation plan around your individual goals. Book online.
